plain_draft:
Slide 1: Tallow Creek Respite Cooperative
In-home respite for unpaid family caregivers
Marrow Junction and the Upper Tallow townships, since 2019
Request to the Ostrander Valley Health Fund, winter caregiving round
$120,000 for one year (FY2027)
Funds an overnight respite pilot and two respite workers in the eastern townships

Slide 2: Wait for a first visit: 41 days down to 12
Average days from referral to first visit: 41 in FY2025, 12 in FY2026
Families on the waitlist at year end: 37 down to 9
Emergency requests filled within 48 hours: 58% (29 of 50) up to 83% (62 of 75)
What changed: worker pay went from $16.50 to $19.00 an hour
Workers who left during the year: 11 of 23 in FY2025, 4 of 31 in FY2026
We also hired a second coordinator and moved scheduling off paper

Slide 3: What we do
Local workers come into the home and stay with an adult who needs supervision
Usually a parent or spouse living with dementia, Parkinson's disease or the after-effects of a stroke
While the worker is there, the caregiver can see a doctor, sleep or rest
FY2026: 171 families, 9,880 respite hours (FY2025: 118 families, 6,240 hours)
Sliding-scale fees from $0 to $14 an hour; 64% of families paid nothing
All-in cost per respite hour: $61.98, down from $68.40
94 cents of every dollar went to delivering or coordinating respite
"For two years I hadn't been to my own doctor. The first Tuesday [our respite worker] came, I went, and I found out I needed the surgery I'd been putting off." (caregiver, Upper Tallow township)

Slide 4: Caregiver strain: a promising result with limits
Measure: 12-item Zarit Burden Interview (scored 0 to 48; higher means more strain)
Average score at intake: 27.4. At six months: 19.8, a drop of 7.6 points
61 caregivers started in the high-strain band (17 or above); 34 of them were below 17 at six months
Read with care:
Only 96 of 171 families completed both surveys, and those who answered may have been doing better
There is no comparison group, and strain often eases for other reasons
Our own coordinators gave the survey
These numbers fit our belief that respite helps, but they do not prove the program caused the drop
FY2027: an outside evaluator will run follow-up surveys, and we will track why families leave

Slide 5: Two gaps we cannot fill today
Nights: 22 families asked for overnight coverage in FY2026, and we could not offer it
Dementia often means wandering, sundowning and lost sleep, and daytime visits do not help with that
Distance: Corliss and Harrow Flat townships made up 9% of referrals but only 4% of respite hours
A worker's round trip to the eastern townships can run 70 miles

Slide 6: FY2027 plan and how we will judge it
Pilot overnight respite for up to 40 families: two 9 p.m. to 7 a.m. shifts a month for six months
Hire two respite workers who live in Corliss and Harrow Flat
Train 14 current workers in dementia care (required for overnight shifts)
Bring in an outside evaluator for follow-up surveys and exit interviews
We will report three measures, even if the results disappoint:
Share of pilot caregivers with at least 5 nights of unbroken sleep a month
Six-month strain scores, collected by the outside evaluator
Whether families keep using the service

Slide 7: FY2027 expansion budget: $165,000
Two eastern township respite workers (2.0 FTE wages and benefits): $96,000
Overnight pilot shift pay (up to 40 families, 6 months): $38,500
Dementia care training for 14 workers: $12,800
Added rural mileage: $9,200
Independent evaluation: $8,500
Total: $165,000
Already committed: $45,000 from the Upper Tallow County Area Agency on Aging (part of the eastern township workers)
Remaining gap and our request: $120,000

Slide 8: Our finances, including our risks
FY2026 revenue: $618,900. Expenses: $612,400. Surplus: $6,500, added to reserve
Operating reserve covers about seven weeks of expenses
County Area Agency on Aging contract: $246,000 (40% of revenue)
Fenwright Family Foundation: $150,000 (24% of revenue)
Together, these two sources make up 64% of our revenue
The Fenwright grant ends its three-year term in FY2027 and will not renew at the same level
Other revenue: individual donors and the Porch Supper (14%), Marrow Junction Community Health Trust (12%), family fees (10%)
Contact: Mirela Aske, Executive Director

P2.text:
Tallow Creek Respite Cooperative
Board meeting notes, Wednesday, November 4, 2026
Present: Osric Pellam (chair), Juniper Haldane (treasurer), Mirela Aske (executive director), Benedikt Orrin (program director)

P4.text: Mirela reported that Teodora Vance, program officer at the Ostrander Valley Health Fund, invited us to submit a short deck for their winter caregiving round after reading our FY2026 report. Ask: $120,000 for one year toward the FY2027 overnight respite pilot and the two eastern township workers. Total expansion cost is $165,000; the county Area Agency on Aging has already committed $45,000.

P5.text: Deadline: deck to Teodora by Tuesday, December 1, 2026. Mirela wants a draft to the board by Friday, November 20.

P6.text: Juniper noted that Fenwright's $150,000 does not renew at the same level after FY2027 and asked that we not hide how much we lean on the county and Fenwright (64 percent). Osric agreed.

P7.text:
Instructions for the deck, agreed by the board:
1. Keep it to eight slides or fewer. Teodora said she reads them on her phone.
2. Lead with the waitlist: 41 days down to 12. That is our strongest number and it is not in dispute.
3. Show the strain result (27.4 to 19.8) only with the caveat in plain view: 96 of 171 families answered, no comparison group, our own staff gave the survey. Do not call the program "evidence-based" and do not say respite keeps people out of nursing homes.
4. Show the full $165,000 by line, with the county's $45,000 visible, so the $120,000 ask is clearly the gap.
5. No photos of caregivers or the people they care for, and no names. The quote can run without attribution beyond "caregiver, Upper Tallow township."

P8.text: Benedikt will pull the numbers. Mirela owns the draft.

P10.text:
## FY2026 Annual Program Report
### July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026 | Marrow Junction and the Upper Tallow townships

P11.text:
Tallow Creek Respite Cooperative gives unpaid family caregivers a few hours of their lives back. We train and employ local respite workers who go into the home and stay with an adult who needs supervision, most often a parent or spouse living with dementia, Parkinson's disease, or the after-effects of a stroke. While the worker is there, the caregiver sees a doctor, sleeps, or sits in a parked car and does nothing at all. We have done this since 2019 with a staff of two coordinators and a pool of part-time workers who live in the communities they serve.
Families pay on a sliding scale from zero to $14 an hour. In FY2026, 64 percent of families paid nothing.

P12.text:
FY2026 was the first full year after we moved scheduling off paper and onto a shared calendar, hired a second coordinator, and raised respite worker pay from $16.50 to $19.00 an hour. The pay raise mattered most. In FY2025 we lost 11 of 23 workers during the year, and every departure put families back on the waitlist. In FY2026 we lost 4 of 31.
| Measure | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Caregiver families served | 118 | 171 |
| Respite hours delivered | 6,240 | 9,880 |
| Average hours per family per month | 4.4 | 4.8 |
| Active respite workers (year end) | 23 | 31 |
| Workers who left during the year | 11 | 4 |
| Average days from referral to first visit | 41 | 12 |
| Emergency requests filled within 48 hours | 58% (29 of 50) | 83% (62 of 75) |
| Families on waitlist at year end | 37 | 9 |

P13.text:
The waitlist number is the one we watch. A caregiver who calls us is usually calling late, after a fall, a hospital stay, or a night without sleep. Forty-one days was too long. Twelve days is still not where we want it, but it is a different service.
Emergency requests, usually a caregiver's own surgery or hospital stay, grew from 50 to 75, and we filled a far larger share.

P14.text:
At intake and again at six months, we ask caregivers to complete the 12-item short form of the Zarit Burden Interview, a widely used questionnaire that scores caregiver strain from 0 to 48. Higher scores mean more strain.
Among the 96 caregivers who completed both an intake and a six-month survey in FY2026, the average score fell from 27.4 to 19.8, a drop of 7.6 points. Sixty-one of the 96 were in the high-strain band (17 or above) at intake; 34 of those 61 were below 17 at six months.
P14.locator: “Caregiver strain: what we found and what we cannot claim”

P15.text: We want funders to read this result carefully. First, only 96 of our 171 families completed the six-month survey. Some families left the program because the person they cared for moved into a nursing home or died; others simply did not return the form. Caregivers who stayed and answered may have been the ones doing better, so the average likely overstates the change. Second, we have no comparison group. Strain often eases for reasons that have nothing to do with us: a diagnosis settles, a sibling steps in, a medication starts working. Third, our coordinators administer the survey, and caregivers may want to give a good answer to the person who sends them help. We believe respite reduces strain, and the direction of these numbers fits that belief, but this is not proof that our program caused the drop.
P15.locator: “Caregiver strain: what we found and what we cannot claim”

P16.text: In FY2027 we will contract with an outside evaluator to run follow-up calls so that the survey is not given by the people who schedule the care, and we will track why families leave.
P16.locator: “Caregiver strain: what we found and what we cannot claim”

P17.text: "For two years I hadn't been to my own doctor. The first Tuesday Ana came, I went, and I found out I needed the surgery I'd been putting off." (Caregiver for her husband, Upper Tallow township)

P18.text:
| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Respite worker wages and benefits | $398,100 |
| Worker training and certification | $34,600 |
| Program coordination (2.0 FTE) | $112,300 |
| Mileage and worker transportation | $29,800 |
| Administration, insurance, and audit | $37,600 |
| **Total expenses** | **$612,400** |
Ninety-four cents of each dollar went to delivering or coordinating respite. Our cost per respite hour, all in, was $61.98, down from $68.40 in FY2025, mostly because coordinator time is now spread over more hours of care.

P19.text:
| Source | Amount | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Upper Tallow County Area Agency on Aging (service contract) | $246,000 | 40% |
| Fenwright Family Foundation (general operating) | $150,000 | 24% |
| Individual donors and the October Porch Supper | $89,000 | 14% |
| Marrow Junction Community Health Trust (worker training) | $75,000 | 12% |
| Sliding-scale family fees | $58,900 | 10% |
| **Total revenue** | **$618,900** | **100%** |
We ended the year with a surplus of $6,500, which went to our operating reserve. The reserve now covers about seven weeks of expenses.
One concern for the board: the county contract and the Fenwright grant together make up 64 percent of our revenue. The Fenwright grant is in its final year of a three-year commitment and will not renew at the same level after FY2027.

P20.text:
Two gaps showed up again and again in our intake calls this year.
The first is nights. Caregivers of people with dementia often lose sleep to wandering and sundowning, and four-hour daytime visits do not touch that. Twenty-two families asked for overnight coverage in FY2026, and we could not offer it.
The second is geography. Families in Corliss and Harrow Flat townships, the far eastern end of the county, made up 9 percent of our referrals but only 4 percent of our respite hours, because a worker's round trip there can run 70 miles.
In FY2027 we will:
P20.locator: “FY2027 plan: overnight respite and the two eastern townships”

P21.text:
1. Pilot overnight respite for up to 40 families, offering two overnight shifts (9 p.m. to 7 a.m.) per family per month for six months.
2. Hire two respite workers who live in Corliss and Harrow Flat.
3. Train 14 current workers in dementia-specific care, required for overnight shifts.
4. Bring in an outside evaluator to run follow-up surveys and exit interviews.
| FY2027 expansion line | Cost |
|---|---|
| Two additional respite workers, eastern townships (2.0 FTE wages and benefits) | $96,000 |
| Overnight pilot shift pay (up to 40 families, 6 months) | $38,500 |
| Dementia care training for 14 workers | $12,800 |
| Added rural mileage | $9,200 |
| Independent evaluation | $8,500 |
| **Total expansion cost** | **$165,000** |
P21.locator: “FY2027 plan: overnight respite and the two eastern townships”

P22.text:
The Upper Tallow County Area Agency on Aging has committed $45,000 toward this expansion through an amendment to our service contract, to cover part of the eastern township workers. We are seeking the remaining $120,000 from philanthropic partners.
If the overnight pilot works, we will know it by three things: the share of pilot caregivers who report at least five nights of unbroken sleep a month, their six-month strain scores gathered by the outside evaluator, and whether the families keep using the service. We will report all three, including if they disappoint.
P22.locator: “FY2027 plan: overnight respite and the two eastern townships”

P23.text: Board Chair: Osric Pellam. Treasurer: Juniper Haldane. Executive Director: Mirela Aske. Program Director: Benedikt Orrin.
